topic: JVM Internals (Memory Model, G1/ZGC, Class Loading)

questions.scenario: You are debugging a production issue where a high-throughput payment microservice running on JDK 17 with the `G1GC` garbage collector experiences intermittent, catastrophic latency spikes (multi-second pauses) under heavy load. A heap dump analysis reveals that the total live set is well below 50% of the 32GB maximum heap size, yet GC logs consistently report `To-space exhausted` followed by Full GC cycles triggered by `Allocation Failure`. The team recently added a feature that writes large, encrypted audit trails formatted as raw `byte[]` arrays (averaging 4MB to 12MB each) directly to disk during each transaction.
questions.question: What is the primary architectural cause of these `To-space exhausted` and Full GC events?
options: A) The default `G1ReservePercent` is completely exhausted by thread stack allocations, forcing G1 to fall back to a serial mark-sweep-compact Full GC.
B) Rapid allocation of Humongous Objects directly into the Old Generation creates contiguous region fragmentation and prematurely exhausts available regions before concurrent marking completes.
C) The JVM Card Table overflowed because write barriers cannot track references spanning across non-adjacent Survivor spaces during bursty allocations.
D) The `InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent` (IHOP) calculation was automatically triggered too early, causing Mixed GC pause times to exceed the target `MaxGCPauseMillis`.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) Rapid allocation of Humongous Objects directly into the Old Generation creates contiguous region fragmentation and prematurely exhausts available regions before concurrent marking completes.
questions.explanation: In G1GC, any allocation larger than 50% of a G1 region size (defaulting between 1MB and 32MB depending on heap size, commonly 16MB for a 32GB heap) is classified as a Humongous Object. Humongous objects bypass the Young generation (Eden/Survivor) and are allocated directly into a contiguous set of regions in the Old generation. High allocation rates of 4MB-12MB byte arrays cause severe heap fragmentation because finding contiguous free regions becomes impossible. When free regions run out and an allocation cannot proceed, G1 cannot evacuate survivor objects (triggering `To-space exhausted`) and degrades into a stop-the-world Full GC to defragment the heap.

questions.question: What is the subtle JMM (Java Memory Model) bug causing this behavior?
options: A) The method `loadConfiguration` executes inside a CGLIB proxy that fails to synchronize on class metadata during class reloading.

B) Due to the absence of memory barriers on `initialized` and `runtimeConfig`, instructions may be reordered, or writes to `runtimeConfig` may remain in CPU store buffers, allowing other threads to observe `initialized == true` before seeing the populated `HashMap` contents.
C) The `HashMap` instance escapes into Metaspace before its internal bucket array is allocated by the JIT compiler.
D) Non-atomic 64-bit reference writes in 64-bit HotSpot cause tearing of the pointer reference to `runtimeConfig` unless the object is marked `@Transactional`.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) Due to the absence of memory barriers on `initialized` and `runtimeConfig`, instructions may be reordered, or writes to `runtimeConfig` may remain in CPU store buffers, allowing other threads to observe `initialized == true` before seeing the populated `HashMap` contents.
questions.explanation: Under the Java Memory Model (JMM), plain non-volatile field reads and writes do not establish a *happens-before* relationship. The compiler and CPU out-of-order execution units are free to reorder the assignment `this.initialized = true` before the internal array initialization and entries of `new HashMap<>(configs)` are fully published to main memory. Reader threads can see `initialized == true` while `runtimeConfig` is still `null`, or observe a partially initialized `HashMap` whose internal table array contains null pointers, triggering a `NullPointerException` or lost updates.

questions.scenario: You are debugging a production issue in an enterprise Spring Boot application that dynamically loads custom tenant plugins at runtime using custom `URLClassLoader` instances. During performance testing where plugins are frequently loaded, executed, and unloaded, the application crashes with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`. Memory metrics show that Metaspace usage grows monotonically. Heap dumps reveal that thousands of `PluginClassLoader` instances and class metadata records are pinned in memory, even though the application explicitly removes all references to the `URLClassLoader` instances and invokes `close()` on them.
questions.question: Which of the following JVM class loading mechanics explains why the `PluginClassLoader` and its loaded classes cannot be garbage collected?
options: A) Metaspace allocations are managed exclusively by the OS C-heap and are only freed upon complete JVM process termination.

B) Instances of classes loaded by `PluginClassLoader` registered a thread or static field tied to a JVM system class loader, or an unclosed `ThreadLocal` on a shared thread pool references a class/instance from that class loader.
C) The G1GC concurrent cycle ignores Metaspace unless explicitly configured with `-XX:+ClassUnloadingWithConcurrentMark` and `-XX:+UseZGC` simultaneously.
D) CGLIB dynamic subclasses generated inside Spring `@Configuration` classes cannot be unloaded if Spring's `DefaultListableBeanFactory` is instantiated in a parent loader.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) Instances of classes loaded by `PluginClassLoader` registered a thread or static field tied to a JVM system class loader, or an unclosed `ThreadLocal` on a shared thread pool references a class/instance from that class loader.
questions.explanation: A class loader can only be garbage-collected along with its loaded classes and Metaspace native memory if all three conditions are met: (1) 0 instances of any class loaded by that classloader exist on the heap, (2) 0 references to the `ClassLoader` itself exist, and (3) no loaded `Class` objects are referenced. A common culprit in plugin architectures is shared thread pools (e.g., Tomcat/Netty request threads): if code executed by the plugin sets a `ThreadLocal` containing a plugin object or class and fails to call `remove()`, the long-lived worker thread maintains a strong reference to that object. The object points to its `Class`, which points to its `PluginClassLoader`, transitively pinning all classes and their associated Metaspace metadata.
